beanstalk.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
beanstalk.role: Deploy an application; let Beanstalk coordinate its infrastructure.
bullets: Standard environments manage EC2, load balancing, scaling, deployment and health.
Use .ebextensions/<name>.config (YAML/JSON) for environment options, instance customization and extra CloudFormation resources.
Environment-created resources normally share its lifecycle; keep durable RDS outside it. A disposable session cache can be recreated.
beanstalk.boundary: Rolling can reduce serving capacity and leave mixed versions after failure. Immutable/traffic splitting replace the fleet and lose accumulated CPU burst credits. Blue/green uses separate environments and a CNAME swap.
beanstalk.example:
option_settings:
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:command:
    DeploymentPolicy: RollingWithAdditionalBatch
    BatchSizeType: Fixed
    BatchSize: 2

# Install a tool on the environment's EC2 instances.
packages:
  yum:
    jq: []

# Provision a managed cache in the environment stack.
Resources:
  SessionCache:
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::CacheCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: memcached
      CacheNodeType: cache.t3.micro
      NumCacheNodes: 1
      CacheSubnetGroupName: example-cache-subnets
      VpcSecurityGroupIds:
        - sg-0123456789abcdef0

rows: May drop to zero; quickest rollout
Reduced by the batch being updated
Keep old fleet intact while validating new

beanstalk.note: Replace the cache subnet group/security group placeholders with compatible existing VPC resources and allow application access to the cache. This excerpt omits network setup; it has no retention policy, so the cache follows environment deletion. On a failed rolling deployment, replacement instances use the last successful app version; redeploy to restore consistency.

ec2.name: Amazon EC2
ec2.role: A virtual machine with OS and instance-level control.
bullets: Linux user-data shell scripts run as root, normally on the first launch boot only. Configure cloud-init explicitly for later boots.
Stop an EBS-backed instance before changing its user-data attribute; changing it does not itself rerun the script.
T-family instances spend CPU credits on bursts; sustained CPU demand needs an appropriate family or credit configuration.
ec2.boundary: Hardware isolation alone points to Dedicated Instances; physical host placement or socket/core licensing points to Dedicated Hosts.
ec2.example:
#!/bin/bash
# Amazon Linux example; first-boot setup, not a recurring job.
dnf install -y nginx
systemctl enable --now nginx

docs.label: Current vs legacy EC2 Free Tier

rows: Dedicated customer hardware; no host placement

asg.name: EC2 Auto Scaling
asg.role: Maintain fleet capacity across AZs; pair with ELB to route traffic.
bullets: One ASG belongs to one Region and uses subnets in one or more AZs. It normally attempts to balance instances across enabled AZs.
The group replaces unhealthy instances and scales instance count in/out. Changing instance size is a separate vertical-scaling operation.
ELB distributes requests across registered targets. Its cross-zone setting controls whether an LB node can route outside its own AZ; it does not rebalance the instance fleet.
asg.boundary: Cross-zone ≠ cross-Region. An ASG and a regional load balancer stay within one Region. Use separate regional stacks plus Route 53 or Global Accelerator for global traffic routing.
asg.note: DesiredCapacity=10 sets the fleet total, not a 2/8 AZ allocation. A launch template supplies AMI, instance type, security groups and bootstrap configuration. Scale against the measured bottleneck.

alb.name: Application Load Balancer
alb.role: Route HTTP requests to healthy targets.
bullets: An internet-facing ALB routes HTTP requests to healthy targets, including targets with private IP addresses.
Health checks have their own path, port, matcher and network reachability; direct access can work while a target is unhealthy.
With cross-zone balancing and equal healthy target weights, 2 targets in AZ A + 8 in AZ B means about 10% per target.
alb.boundary: ALB access logs describe requests. CloudWatch metrics aggregate measurements. CloudTrail describes AWS API/account activity.

rows: Which client, URL, status and target timing?
Request details; not the application body or a complete audit ledger
Who changed a listener or security setting?
Administrative AWS API activity; not each HTTP request
Check path, port, matcher, security groups and NACLs

alb.note: Request tracing supplies an X-Amzn-Trace-Id for correlation; instrumentation is still needed for downstream spans. The 10% example assumes request-count routing, not differing target weights, stickiness or connection behaviour.

apigw.name: Amazon API Gateway
apigw.role: Expose an API with routing, integration and access controls.
bullets: A stage is a named environment pointing to an API deployment snapshot. A canary tests a newer deployment on the same stage URL.
Stage variables configure integrations; VTL mapping templates transform payloads. A proxy integration instead passes its standard event to the backend.
Authorizers establish caller access. Usage plans meter API-key consumers; caching can avoid repeated backend work.
apigw.boundary: API keys are not authentication. Usage-plan quotas/throttles are best effort, not hard spend limits. Verify the API type before selecting a feature.
apigw.exampleTitle: Control-plane example · create a usage plan (API request body)
apigw.note: Create or import PartnerApp’s API key, then attach it to this plan separately. Mark GET /GetOrder as API Key Required. Both stages share this example’s per-key limits; the key does not route traffic. Quotas/throttles are best effort. Cache only safely scoped responses, with TTL/invalidation appropriate for changes in data and entitlements.

lambda.name: AWS Lambda
lambda.role: Execute event-driven code without operating a conventional server fleet.
bullets: For conventional Lambda compute, memory is 128–10,240 MB; CPU grows with memory, with about one vCPU at 1,769 MB.
Layers share code/dependencies and custom runtime content; they do not allocate extra CPU.
Published versions are immutable. $LATEST is unpublished. An alias points to a published version and can weight a second version.
lambda.boundary: Call the alias to use its routing policy. An alias cannot point to another alias. A new version alone does not create a canary.

rows: Independent CPU selector for this compute mode

lambda.note: Rollback: remove additional weights and route prod to v1. Measure duration and cost together. Lambda Managed Instances has different compute configuration; do not generalize this memory-only rule to every Lambda offering.

cfn.name: AWS CloudFormation
cfn.role: Provision related resources as a versioned stack.
bullets: Resources is required. Parameters, Mappings, Conditions, Outputs and Transform are optional sections.
DependsOn is a resource attribute; there is no top-level Dependencies section. Ref/GetAtt also create implicit dependencies.
Conditions gate resources/outputs or property values through Fn::If. Parameters supply inputs; a Condition cannot be attached to a parameter.
cfn.boundary: Export names are unique per account/Region. Standard Fn::ImportValue references stay in that account/Region; an active import prevents changing/deleting the exported value.
cfn.example:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]
Resources:
  Orders:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: !If [IsProd, 1209600, 345600]
Outputs:
  QueueArn:
    Value: !GetAtt Orders.Arn
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-QueueArn'

rows: Parameter value or resource-specific return value

cfn.note: StackSets deploy a template across selected accounts/Regions with parameters and permissions. This is different from a same-Region export/import dependency. Consult current docs for newer cross-Region output-reference features.

cdk.name: AWS CDK
cdk.role: Define AWS infrastructure using programming-language constructs.
bullets: Compose constructs into stacks/apps using TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#/.NET or Go.
cdk synth produces CloudFormation templates; cdk deploy uses CloudFormation to create or update the stack.
Covers serverless and other infrastructure: Lambda, APIs, VPCs, EC2, ECS, databases and more. Reusable constructs can generate many resources.
cdk.boundary: CDK is not a runtime and is not limited to servers. SAM and CDK both describe infrastructure; choose serverless YAML shorthand/local tooling versus general programming-language composition.
cdk.example:
from aws_cdk import Stack, aws_lambda as lambda_
from constructs import Construct

class OrdersStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, construct_id: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        lambda_.Function(self, "Orders",
            runtime=lambda_.Runtime.PYTHON_3_13,
            handler="app.handler",
            code=lambda_.Code.from_asset("src"))

rows: Deployment unit that maps to a CloudFormation stack
Generate CloudFormation; does not start a production application

cdk.exampleTitle: CDK stack excerpt · creates a Lambda function
cdk.note: cdk init → write constructs → build if needed → cdk synth → cdk deploy. SAM can also declare ordinary CloudFormation resources; serverless scope versus broad infrastructure is a preference, not an absolute capability boundary.

sam.name: AWS SAM
sam.role: Define, build, test and deploy a serverless application.
bullets: The SAM template extends CloudFormation; Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 expands shorthand into deployable resources.
The SAM CLI builds/packages code, invokes supported functions locally, emulates supported API routes and deploys through CloudFormation.
Mix AWS::Serverless::* shorthand with standard AWS::* resources in the same template. The resulting Lambda functions/API/database run in AWS.
sam.boundary: SAM is infrastructure and development tooling, not compute. AWS::Serverless::UserPool is invalid; use AWS::Cognito::UserPool. Local testing does not reproduce every cloud behavior.
sam.example:
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Resources:
  Handler:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Runtime: python3.13
      Handler: app.handler
      CodeUri: src/
      Events:
        GetOrder:
          Type: HttpApi
          Properties:
            Path: /GetOrder
            Method: GET
  Users:
    Type: AWS::Cognito::UserPool

rows: Lambda function + supported events, permissions and deployment settings
A DynamoDB table with simplified configuration
Nested/reusable serverless application, including SAR applications

sam.exampleTitle: SAM template excerpt · HTTP API + Lambda + standard Cognito resource
sam.note: sam init → sam build → sam local invoke / sam local start-api → sam deploy --guided. The table lists common types; the current reference includes additional shorthand resources. SAM remains explicit in exam skills 3.2.4, 3.3.1, 3.3.4 and 3.4.3.

sar.name: AWS Serverless Application Repository
sar.role: Find, share and deploy versioned reusable serverless applications.
bullets: Applications package a SAM template with deployment artifacts; choose an application version and supply its parameters.
Publish privately for a team/organization or publicly, subject to sharing permissions.
AWS::Serverless::Application can reference a repository application; deployment creates the underlying application resources.
sar.boundary: SAR is an application repository, not compute. Service Catalog governs approved products; AWS Marketplace distributes third-party software/services.
sar.example:
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Resources:
  SharedApplication:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Application
    Properties:
      Location:
        ApplicationId: arn:aws:serverlessrepo:us-east-1:123456789012:applications/example-app
        SemanticVersion: 1.0.0
sar.exampleTitle: Reference a SAR application · illustrative ARN/version
sar.note: Replace the application ARN/version, grant required access and provide the application’s required parameters. Inspect the template and permissions before deployment.

dynamodb.name: Amazon DynamoDB
dynamodb.role: Key-value/document storage organized around key-based access.
bullets: GameName + Version identifies a game version; querying GameName returns its versions. Category + GameName on a GSI supports category lookup.
A GSI only returns projected attributes; use ALL when the index must return every game attribute. GSI reads are eventually consistent.
TTL is a Number containing Unix seconds. Expiration is asynchronous cleanup; TTL deletions can appear in Streams. Filter expired data when required.
dynamodb.boundary: Read-then-write can race. Use an atomic conditional write for a request ID, then coordinate status/results with business side effects.

rows: Hot keys and service quotas still apply
Throttle if capacity is insufficient; consider Auto Scaling

dynamodb.note: The key schema must make RequestId the primary key in this separate ledger. A successful claim does not prove the payment/write completed; persist outcomes and recover abandoned work. A String Version sorts lexically; use Number or suitable encoding for numeric ordering.

sqs.name: Amazon SQS
sqs.role: Buffer work so consumers can process it independently.
bullets: Receive hides a message; DeleteMessage acknowledges success. Default visibility is 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours; duplicates still require idempotency.
PurgeQueue removes messages and keeps the queue. DeleteQueue removes both. RemovePermission edits queue-policy permission.
Choose queue type at creation; it cannot be converted later. Source and DLQ types must match. Queue tags are case-sensitive.
sqs.boundary: VisibilityTimeout hides received work; DelaySeconds postpones initial availability; MessageRetentionPeriod limits retention. They are different clocks.

rows: Ordered within a message group; producer deduplication

sqs.note: Backlog per worker = ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible / running workers. Target backlog = acceptable wait / average processing time. Apply target tracking to ECS with an appropriate task-count metric and a scale-from-zero strategy.

kinesis.name: Kinesis Data Streams
kinesis.role: Retain continuous events in shard lanes for independent, replayable reads.
bullets: A stream contains shards; shards contain records. Partition keys map records to a shard, where Kinesis assigns sequence numbers.
PutRecords batches records. HTTP 200 can include partial failures: inspect FailedRecordCount and each result; retry only failed entries with backoff and jitter.
ProvisionedThroughputExceededException indicates capacity/hot-key pressure; InternalFailure is a service-side record error. Preserve an application event ID for deduplication.
kinesis.boundary: Spreading partition keys can fix a hot shard. Increasing provisioned shards can add capacity; merging shards or sending more requests does not fix producer throttling.

rows: Scaling boundaries, hot keys and quotas still apply

kinesis.exampleTitle: PutRecords response: retry the second input record
kinesis.note: Results align with request order. PutRecords does not guarantee ordering across successful and retried records. Reducing readers does not directly fix producer-side write throttling.

containers.name: Amazon ECS
containers.role: Orchestrate container tasks and services; choose their compute separately.
bullets: ECS schedules tasks/services. A task definition is the container blueprint; a service maintains the desired tasks. EC2 and Fargate are distinct capacity choices.
Task-local ephemeral/bind-mount data is suitable for temporary files. EC2 host volumes depend on host lifecycle.
EFS provides persistent shared network files for supported ECS/Fargate tasks across AZs. Configure mount targets, NFS access and file permissions.
containers.boundary: A local volume is not a shared cross-AZ filesystem. Fargate EFS support requires a supported Linux platform; do not assume every OS/launch mode supports it.
containers.note: The excerpt omits task roles, CPU/memory, networking and other required task settings. Add an EFS access point/IAM authorization where needed; a mount declaration alone does not grant access.

fargate.name: AWS Fargate
fargate.role: Supply managed compute capacity for containers without managing EC2 hosts.
bullets: For ECS, define the image, task CPU/memory, networking and roles; Fargate supplies isolated task compute.
ECS still schedules tasks/services. You continue to own the container, IAM permissions, security groups and application behavior.
Task-local storage is ephemeral. Use supported EFS integration when tasks need shared persistent files.
fargate.boundary: Fargate is container compute; ECS is orchestration. Fargate does not build images or define infrastructure templates. Choose self-managed EC2 capacity when host-level requirements demand it.

rows: Managed task compute; supported CPU/memory/platform combinations
Discounted interruptible capacity; design interruption-tolerant work

fargate.note: Add task execution/application roles and the network configuration when launching tasks. The task execution role covers supported agent actions such as image pulls; the task role grants permissions to application code.

rds.name: Amazon RDS
rds.role: Managed relational databases with SQL and transactions.
bullets: Read replicas asynchronously copy data; the application must send reads to replica endpoints. Expect possible replication lag.
A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance has a standby for failover, not reads.
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable standby DB instances; engine/configuration support matters.
rds.boundary: Read load points to replicas; failover points to Multi-AZ; repeated reusable results may point to a cache. These choices can coexist.
rds.example:
# Application routing, not an AWS API payload
write_connection = connect(primary_endpoint)
report_connection = connect(read_replica_endpoint)
# Use the primary for reads that require the latest committed value.

cache.name: Amazon ElastiCache
cache.role: Keep frequently reused data in memory.
bullets: Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached support low-latency cached access; choose engine capabilities deliberately.
A cache hit can reduce database work. A miss still needs a source-of-truth lookup.
Use expiry and invalidation to manage staleness. Memcached is not a durable primary database.
cache.boundary: A cache endpoint does not execute relational SQL in place of RDS. Cache-aside requires application logic and a key design.

rows: Provisioned nodes; reservation options where supported

iam.name: IAM, STS & Access Analyzer
iam.role: Establish AWS trust and evaluate permissions.
bullets: Identity policies grant actions; supported resource policies grant access to resources. A role trust policy says who may assume it; STS issues temporary credentials.
Permissions boundaries and SCPs limit applicable permissions; they do not grant actions. An explicit applicable deny overrides an allow.
Access Analyzer finds supported external/unused access and validates policies. Policy variables can scope reusable access, e.g. an IAM user’s own S3 prefix.
iam.boundary: Trusting an identity does not authorize every resource. ${aws:username} is for IAM users and is not generally present for role sessions; use suitable principal tags/identity variables.
iam.note: Billing-console access can require the account root user to Activate IAM Access plus appropriate IAM permissions. SCPs govern member-account principals within their documented scope; they are not a universal policy attached to every possible caller.

network.name: Security groups & NACLs
network.role: Filter network traffic at two different boundaries.
bullets: Security groups attach to network interfaces and are stateful: allowed traffic automatically permits its response.
NACLs operate at subnet boundaries and are stateless: allow the required request and return traffic, including ephemeral ports.
Check routes, security groups, NACLs, listener and target health separately when diagnosing connectivity.
network.boundary: Network reachability does not authenticate a user or grant an IAM action. Security groups use allow rules only; NACLs support allow and deny.
network.example:
client --HTTPS 443--> public ALB
ALB security group --app port--> private target security group
subnet NACL: allow request + return-port traffic both ways

s3.name: Amazon S3 encryption
s3.role: Store objects; enforce the encryption contract at upload.
bullets: New S3 uploads are encrypted by default. SSE-S3 uses AES256; SSE-KMS uses aws:kms in the encryption request header.
Default bucket encryption chooses storage encryption even when the client omits a header.
A bucket policy can require an explicit mode/key. Missing-header checks and incorrect-value checks express different requirements.
s3.boundary: Requiring a request header rejects clients that rely on bucket defaults. Requiring aws:kms alone does not pin a particular KMS key; validate its key ID/ARN when required.

rows: KMS policy/use permissions; KMS charges may apply

s3.note: Illustrative bucket name. This narrow policy shows request enforcement, not complete bucket access. KMS upload/download permissions and bucket policies must also allow the intended principal.

kms.name: AWS KMS
kms.role: Control cryptographic keys and cryptographic operations.
bullets: Use a KMS key directly for supported small payloads; use envelope encryption for larger application data.
GenerateDataKey returns plaintext and encrypted copies of a data key. Encrypt data locally, discard plaintext key, store the encrypted key with ciphertext.
Normal crypto calls do not return the underlying KMS key material. Rotation support depends on key type/origin; rotating key material is not recreating a key per request.
kms.boundary: Encryption does not replace authorization. A principal needs the relevant service access and KMS key-use authorization; cross-account use requires compatible policies.
kms.example:
# Envelope encryption, conceptual flow
plain_key, encrypted_key = kms.generate_data_key(key_id, key_spec="AES_256")
ciphertext = authenticated_encrypt(plain_key, document)
securely_discard(plain_key)
store(ciphertext, encrypted_key)
# Later: KMS Decrypt(encrypted_key) → data key → decrypt document.

cognito.name: Amazon Cognito
cognito.role: Authenticate application users; federate them into AWS access when needed.
bullets: User pools provide a user directory/federation and issue ID/access JWTs plus refresh tokens.
Identity pools exchange supported identities for temporary AWS credentials, including narrowly scoped guest access when enabled.
API Gateway can authorize with Cognito tokens; a Lambda authorizer supports custom token validation/rules. HTTP APIs have native JWT authorizers.
cognito.boundary: A user-pool JWT is not an access key. A browser may call your API with a bearer token, while the backend calls AWS with its own role credentials.
cognito.example:
# Authenticated application → protected API
Authorization: Bearer <access-token-JWT>

# Direct AWS SDK access uses temporary credentials instead
{"AccessKeyId":"<temporary-id>",
 "SecretKey":"<temporary-secret>",
 "SessionToken":"<session-token>",
 "Expiration":"<expiry>"}

rows: User pool (+ external IdP if needed)

cognito.note: Validate token signature, issuer, audience/client binding, token_use and expiry; apply required scopes and record/tenant rules. User and identity pools can be combined. Never place a secret credential in a public client bundle.

secrets.name: Secrets Manager & Parameter Store
bullets: Secrets Manager stores secrets and supports automatic rotation through service-managed integrations or Lambda workflows, depending on secret type.
Parameter Store stores named configuration, versions and encrypted SecureString values; it has no equivalent native database-password rotation workflow.
Grant runtime roles narrow read/decrypt access. Retrieve and cache values appropriately; do not embed secrets in code or logs.
secrets.boundary: Rotating RDS credentials points to Secrets Manager. An expiration notification/parameter policy is not a password-rotation implementation.
secrets.example:
# AWS CLI; never print this result in application logs
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/orders/endpoint
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/orders/token --with-decryption

rows: Per secret + API use; integration-specific rotation
Standard storage free; throughput options may bill

secrets.note: SecureString needs appropriate KMS permissions. Parameter Store can reference a Secrets Manager secret as a pass-through; the rotation capability still belongs to Secrets Manager.

evidence.name: CloudWatch, CloudTrail & tracing
evidence.role: Choose evidence that can actually answer the question.
bullets: CloudWatch metrics show aggregate demand/latency/errors; Logs hold application events when configured.
ALB access logs show client IP, path, timing and status. CloudTrail shows supported AWS API/account events, not every HTTP request.
Trace IDs correlate requests; distributed tracing reveals downstream latency when the application/services are instrumented.
evidence.boundary: Check target health settings and reachability before scaling an unhealthy target. Adding capacity does not fix a wrong health-check path or denied request.
evidence.example:
symptom: HTTP 5xx increased after deployment
1. CloudWatch: when, how many, ALB or target errors?
2. ALB access logs: which path / target / status / timing?
3. Trace + app log: which dependency failed?
4. CloudTrail: who changed the configuration?
evidence.note: CloudTrail data events are service/operation-specific and often require explicit enablement. They do not replace application access logs. Avoid sensitive credentials/payloads in diagnostic logs.

pipeline.name: AWS CodePipeline
pipeline.role: Coordinate the stages that turn a source revision into a release.
bullets: Source, build/test, approval and deploy actions form an orchestrated delivery workflow.
CodePipeline passes artifacts and invokes action providers. CodeBuild runs build commands; CloudFormation and CodeDeploy perform their respective deployment actions.
A pipeline service role and action-specific permissions authorize delivery. They are separate from the runtime application role.
pipeline.boundary: A successful pipeline action proves that action succeeded; verify which artifact, configuration and route are actually serving production.

rows: Compare action-execution pricing; see current rates

pipeline.note: This is one stage, not a complete CreatePipeline request. Source connection, roles, artifact storage and deploy actions are configured elsewhere.

build.name: AWS CodeBuild
build.role: Run build/test commands and produce a deployable artifact.
bullets: The buildspec defines phases, commands and artifact output. A managed build environment runs those commands.
Package Lambda ZIPs or container images for the target runtime. S3 stores build artifacts; ECR stores container images; CodeArtifact stores software packages.
Run unit/integration tests and inspect their results. Amazon Q Developer can assist with code and tests; developers still review and validate the result.
build.boundary: Compiling code is not deploying it. A passing unit test does not prove the production integration, IAM permissions or active route are correct.
build.example:
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - pip install -r requirements.txt -t package/
  build:
    commands:
      - python -m pytest tests/
      - cp app.py package/
      - cd package && zip -r ../function.zip .
artifacts:
  files:
    - function.zip

rows: Flexible build environment without a standing fleet
Manage a fleet for predictable build demand
Supported runtimes, features and duration limits

build.exampleTitle: buildspec.yml for an illustrative Python project
build.note: The example assumes a suitable Linux build image with pytest and zip available, and the named project files. Pin dependencies and select compute from measured build requirements.

deploy.name: AWS CodeDeploy
deploy.role: Roll out an application revision using a platform-specific deployment contract.
bullets: Supports EC2/on-premises, Lambda and ECS deployment platforms.
The AppSpec describes target resources and lifecycle hooks. Deployment configuration controls rollout; configured alarms/hooks support validation and recovery.
Lambda traffic shifting moves an alias between published versions. ECS blue/green shifts service traffic; EC2 deployments can update in place or use replacements.
deploy.boundary: CloudFormation manages declared resources and can deploy application resources/code. CodeDeploy specializes in rollout, hooks and traffic shifting; it does not build the artifact.
deploy.example:
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - OrdersFunction:
      Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
      Properties:
        Name: orders
        Alias: prod
        CurrentVersion: '1'
        TargetVersion: '2'

rows: Blue/green task sets and traffic routing

deploy.note: The deployment group, service role, traffic policy, alarms and optional hooks are configured separately. Verify the actual alias/target and business health before considering a release complete.

events.name: EventBridge & SNS
events.role: Route events or fan a publication out to independent consumers.
bullets: EventBridge connects event sources to matching targets; bus and feature selection determine supported routing/replay behavior.
SNS publishes to topics and pushes to subscribed endpoints. An SNS-to-SQS fanout gives consumers independent queues.
A consumer needs its own authorization, retry and idempotency handling. An accepted publication does not prove the business work completed.
events.boundary: A router or topic does not retain the progress of a multi-step business workflow. A queue buffers pending work; a state machine coordinates steps.

rows: EventBridge bus and matching target configuration
SNS/EventBridge delivery to separate SQS queues

events.note: This illustrates the JSON PutEvents contract for a compatible configured bus. Check per-entry publication results and the exact bus mode; current EventBridge bus types have different feature contracts.

workflow.name: AWS Step Functions
workflow.role: Coordinate application steps with explicit state and failure handling.
bullets: A state machine expresses service calls, branching and supported waits/retries/catches.
Lambda or ECS executes task code; Step Functions retains workflow progress. The workflow execution role needs target-service permissions.
Choose workflow type from duration, integration and execution-semantics requirements; make external side effects idempotent.
workflow.boundary: CodePipeline coordinates software delivery; Step Functions coordinates application/business work. A workflow is optional when one handler or independent consumers suffice.

rows: Durable execution, up to one year; supported callback/job integrations
Short high-volume execution, up to five minutes; integration differences

workflow.exampleTitle: Amazon States Language: one application task
workflow.note: The sample omits retries and business error handling. Workflow execution semantics do not make an external payment exactly once; plan for uncertain task outcomes and replay.

appconfig.name: AWS AppConfig
appconfig.role: Validate and gradually deploy application configuration or feature flags.
bullets: Separate configuration data from the code artifact so supported behavior can change without rebuilding code.
Validators check configuration; deployment strategies control rollout. Configured monitoring can trigger recovery.
Applications retrieve configuration through supported agents/APIs. Parameter Store and Secrets Manager have different storage/rotation responsibilities.
appconfig.boundary: Creating a configuration version does not make every running process use it. Verify deployment, environment and application retrieval/cache behavior.
appconfig.note: The application, environment, profile, validators, deployment strategy and monitoring must already be configured. Current pricing depends on retrieval/deployment usage; check AWS rates for the chosen retrieval pattern.

release.title: Release without losing the requirement
release.question: What must stay safe during deployment?

options.when: No extra instances; reduced capacity acceptable
Keep baseline capacity; update in batches
Keep old fleet intact during validation
Test a percentage on a new fleet
Route a stable function name across versions

release.foot: Blue/green uses separate environments. Keep persistent data outside disposable application environments.

author.title: Infrastructure authoring
author.question: What are you trying to express?

options.when: Reusable infrastructure in a programming language

author.foot: A template, a deployed stack and an application version are different objects.

runtime.title: Runtime and front door
runtime.question: Which responsibility is required?

options.then: ECS; choose EC2 or Fargate capacity

options.when: HTTP API features, identity or transformation
options.then: API Gateway; check REST vs HTTP

options.when: Route HTTP to healthy private targets

runtime.foot: Configure the health-check contract separately from user routes. Network reachability and authorization are separate checks.

data.title: Data access and state
data.question: Which access pattern is the deciding clue?

options.when: Known partition/key lookup; flexible item fields
options.then: DynamoDB; add GSI for another query key
RDS read replica; route reads explicitly
RDS Multi-AZ; know instance vs cluster

data.foot: A cache is not a SQL endpoint. An eventually consistent replica/index is not an immediate-read guarantee.

async.title: Buffer, stream and retries
async.question: What is the delivery requirement?

options.when: Replay stream records; ordered per shard

options.then: Inspect results; retry failed records only
Target backlog per worker, not raw depth

async.foot: Backoff with jitter handles transient pressure. It does not repair invalid requests or authorize denied calls.

access.title: Authenticate, then authorize
access.question: What does the caller need?

options.when: Lambda code calls another AWS service

options.then: Tenancy or network controls, alongside IAM

access.foot: A trusted token proves a supported identity; IAM permissions and application entitlements still need explicit enforcement.

protect.title: Keys, secrets and evidence
protect.question: What must the control do?

options.when: Require explicit S3 upload encryption mode

options.then: Envelope encryption with a data key

options.when: Store named static config or SecureString
Request detail vs aggregate vs admin change
options.then: Access logs vs metrics vs CloudTrail

protect.foot: Encryption, authorization and observability operate at different boundaries; choose each for its own obligation.

delivery-tools.title: Which delivery responsibility?
delivery-tools.question: What must this stage actually do?

options.when: Release code / shift traffic / run hooks

delivery-tools.foot: These tools can cooperate. The deployer role, runtime role and end-user identity remain separate.

events-workflow.title: Route, buffer or coordinate?
events-workflow.question: What state does the service own?

options.when: Which jobs are waiting for a worker?
Which records can a consumer replay?

events-workflow.foot: A producer can publish directly to a queue or stream. Use only the routing, buffering and coordination the application needs.

deployments.name: All at once
deployments.traffic: Requests may fail while all eight instances update.
deployments.rollback: Redeploy the previous application version; the old fleet was updated in place.

deployments.name: Rolling
deployments.traffic: Six old-version instances serve while a batch of two updates.
deployments.rule: No extra instances, but temporary capacity reduction.
deployments.rollback: A failed rollout can leave mixed versions. Redeploy a known version to restore consistency.

deployments.name: Rolling + additional batch
deployments.traffic: Two healthy new instances join before a batch of two old instances updates.
deployments.rule: Preserve baseline serving capacity with one extra batch.
deployments.rollback: Recover/redeploy consistently; this is still a batched rollout, not an untouched full old fleet.

deployments.name: Immutable
deployments.traffic: Old fleet keeps serving while the replacement fleet passes health checks; no user-configured canary percentage.
deployments.rule: Validate a separate fleet before replacing the old one.
deployments.rollback: If candidate health fails, terminate the new fleet and retain the old fleet.

deployments.name: Traffic splitting
deployments.traffic: During evaluation: 90% → old fleet; 10% → candidate fleet (illustrative).
deployments.rule: Measure a candidate with a controlled traffic percentage; ALB required.
deployments.rollback: On failed health or abort, send traffic back to the old fleet and remove the candidate.

identity.name: User → application API
identity.boundary: Public client → trusted identity issuer → API → application data
identity.trust: The API validates the trusted issuer, signature, expected client/audience binding, token type and expiry.
identity.permission: The API must allow the requested scope/route; the application still checks the requested record or tenant.
identity.failureTrust: Reject the token at the API boundary; sign-in elsewhere does not make it trusted here.
identity.failurePermission: A valid token reaches the policy boundary but does not authorize the requested action/data.
identity.success: The user may perform this application operation. Any backend AWS call uses the backend role, not this JWT.

identity.name: User → AWS resource directly
identity.boundary: Public client → identity federation → AWS IAM resource boundary
identity.trust: The identity pool accepts this provider/token; the role trust policy permits the intended federation path.
identity.permission: Role/resource/key policies allow the exact operation and resource; applicable boundaries and organizational controls permit it.
identity.failureTrust: No usable role credentials are issued for this identity/path.
identity.failurePermission: Credentials can exist while the AWS operation is denied by permissions or guardrails.
identity.success: The SDK signs the allowed AWS request with temporary credentials. A raw JWT is not substituted for SigV4.

identity.name: Lambda → AWS service
identity.boundary: Trusted AWS service → function execution role → target AWS resource
flow: 3. SDK credential provider obtains temporary credentials
4. Signed request; evaluate role + resource policy
identity.trust: The execution-role trust policy allows the Lambda service to assume it.
identity.permission: The role and applicable resource/key policies allow the action; guardrails permit it. The app separately enforces its user’s entitlement.
identity.failureTrust: The function cannot use the intended execution role.
identity.failurePermission: Function code can run but its downstream AWS request receives AccessDenied.
identity.success: The SDK calls the target as the execution-role session. The app user does not inherit that role’s permissions.
identity.contract: SDK default credential chain → temporary role credentials → SigV4

practice.title: Preserve fleet capacity
practice.prompt: A Beanstalk Standard environment has eight busy instances. The team wants batched deployments, can afford two temporary instances, and must keep eight serving. Which policy fits?
options: Rolling
Rolling with additional batch
All at once
Immutable
practice.why: An additional batch joins before an existing batch leaves service. Rolling alone reduces capacity; immutable launches a full replacement fleet, exceeding the stated temporary budget.
practice.change: Choose immutable when the full old fleet must remain untouched and a parallel fleet is acceptable.

practice.title: JWT or AWS credentials?
practice.prompt: A mobile app already signs users in with a Cognito user pool. It must upload directly to a permitted S3 prefix using the AWS SDK. What is missing?
options: Send the user-pool JWT as the S3 Authorization header
Create an API key
Configure an identity pool and scoped IAM role; obtain temporary credentials
Use the KMS key as an access token
practice.why: A supported identity is exchanged for temporary AWS credentials. The SDK signs the S3 request; role/resource/KMS permissions still apply. A JWT by itself is not that credential set.
practice.change: If uploads go through a backend API, use its bearer-token authorization and let the backend access S3 with its own role.

practice.title: HTTP success, record failure
practice.prompt: PutRecords returns HTTP 200 with FailedRecordCount = 1. The second result has ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. What should the producer do?
options: Treat the whole request as successful
Retry every input immediately
Merge shards and increase request frequency
Retry the second input with backoff and jitter; inspect partition distribution/capacity
practice.why: The batch response reports per-record outcomes. Retrying only failed entries avoids replaying known successes; partition distribution and capacity determine whether pressure persists.
practice.change: A malformed record needs correction rather than repeated transient-error retries.

practice.title: Condition location
practice.prompt: A CloudFormation template should create an extra queue only in prod. Environment is a parameter. Which approach is valid?
options: Attach Condition to the parameter
Add a top-level Dependencies section
Define a condition using the parameter and attach it to the queue resource
Use StackSets for a conditional queue
practice.why: Parameters supply input; Conditions evaluate it. A resource-level Condition controls creation. DependsOn expresses resource dependencies and is unrelated to the environment test.
practice.change: Use Fn::If when a resource remains present but one property changes by environment.

practice.title: Expiry versus deletion
practice.prompt: A DynamoDB item has a TTL timestamp that passed one minute ago. The application must never return expired offers. What is correct?
options: The TTL service guarantees the item is already deleted
Enforce expiry in reads/business logic; TTL cleans up asynchronously
Change the timestamp to milliseconds
Use a GSI for immediate deletion
practice.why: TTL is asynchronous deletion and uses Unix seconds. Expired items can remain readable until cleanup, so enforce the application validity rule separately.
practice.change: If the requirement is durable background cleanup rather than exact-time validity, TTL may provide that lifecycle alone.

practice.title: SQL read scaling
practice.prompt: A relational application has slow reporting reads but writes are healthy. It must keep SQL queries and can accept some lag. Which change most directly adds read capacity?
options: Traditional Multi-AZ DB instance standby
Read replica and route reports to its endpoint
Send SQL to Memcached
Add an SQS queue without changing readers
practice.why: Read replicas serve reads but the application must direct those queries to them. A traditional Multi-AZ standby supports failover; a cache needs a different application access pattern.
practice.change: Choose Multi-AZ for availability; use the primary when a read must immediately reflect its write.

practice.title: Consumer key versus sign-in
practice.prompt: A REST API needs per-consumer usage plans and must authenticate customers. Which statement is correct?
options: API keys satisfy both requirements
Usage-plan quotas are guaranteed hard limits
Use API keys for usage plans and a suitable authorizer for access
Stage variables authenticate consumers
practice.why: API keys identify consumers for usage plans. Authorizers or IAM establish permitted access. Quotas/throttles are best effort and should not be treated as a hard budget boundary.
practice.change: For a simpler API without usage-plan features, an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer may fit.

practice.title: Healthy directly, unhealthy behind ALB
practice.prompt: An instance serves the homepage directly but fails ALB health checks. What should be checked first?
options: Create a second Region in the ASG
Increase Lambda memory
Buy a Dedicated Host
Health-check path, port, success matcher, security groups and NACL return traffic
practice.why: A working user route does not prove the independent health-check route or its network path works. More capacity repeats the same misconfiguration.
practice.change: Scale after evidence shows healthy targets are capacity constrained rather than failing the health-check contract.

practice.title: Memory or layers?
practice.prompt: A conventional Lambda function is CPU-bound at 128 MB. What is the most direct configuration experiment?
options: Add a layer to allocate a CPU
Increase memory and compare duration/cost
Point an alias at another alias
Increase SQS retention
practice.why: For this compute mode, CPU grows with memory. A layer distributes dependencies. Benchmark to decide whether reduced duration offsets the larger memory allocation.
practice.change: If initialization latency is the measured problem, investigate initialization and supported pre-initialization options instead.

practice.title: Avoid concurrent duplicate writes
practice.prompt: Two workers may process the same payment request simultaneously. Which is the strongest starting point?
options: Read a ledger, then write it without a condition
Assume FIFO means the business side effect can never repeat
Conditionally claim the request ID atomically, then persist/recover its outcome
Set TTL to the current millisecond
practice.why: An atomic condition prevents two concurrent claim winners. The ledger must still coordinate completion, retries and uncertain external side effects; the claim alone is not exactly-once payment execution.
practice.change: For a read-only operation, duplicate execution may be acceptable and a side-effect ledger may be unnecessary.

practice.title: Shared files after task replacement
practice.prompt: Supported Linux Fargate tasks in multiple AZs must use the same persistent files after task replacement. Which storage fits?
options: A task-local temporary directory
A host-local Docker volume
Instance user data
Amazon EFS with appropriate mounts and access controls
practice.why: EFS provides shared network file storage independent of task replacement. Local task/host storage has different scope and lifecycle.
practice.change: Use ephemeral storage for scratch files that can disappear with the task.

practice.title: Store and rotate credentials
practice.prompt: An application needs automatically rotated RDS credentials with the appropriate supported integration. Which is the best starting point?
options: A Parameter Store expiration notification
Secrets Manager rotation with runtime secret retrieval
Hardcode the password in an encrypted AMI
Use the same new KMS key for every request
practice.why: Secrets Manager provides rotation mechanisms appropriate to the secret/integration, updating the stored credential and target system. A parameter expiry notification does not implement password rotation.
practice.change: For static non-secret endpoints or AMI IDs, Parameter Store is a simpler configuration fit.

practice.title: Default encryption or explicit header?
practice.prompt: A requirement says every S3 client upload must explicitly request SSE-KMS. The bucket already defaults to SSE-KMS. What is still needed?
options: Nothing; default storage encryption proves the client sent a header
Deny s3:GetObject only
Enforce the required PutObject encryption header with missing/incorrect-value conditions
Set the upload header to AES256
practice.why: Bucket defaults encrypt stored objects but do not establish what a client explicitly requested. Enforce the request contract separately; pin the KMS key too if required.
practice.change: If only the resulting encryption mode matters, a correctly configured bucket default may satisfy that narrower obligation.

practice.title: Regional reference boundary
practice.prompt: A stack in ap-southeast-2 exports a subnet ID. Another stack tries to use Fn::ImportValue in us-east-1. What is the issue?
options: Export names must be unique across all AWS accounts
Standard ImportValue only reads exports in the same account and Region
FindInMap automatically copies the subnet to another Region
A Ref automatically makes any resource global
practice.why: Standard export/import references share values within one account and Region. StackSets can deploy templates across Regions, but a subnet remains regional.
practice.change: Use an appropriate current cross-Region output/configuration mechanism when that is the actual requirement; do not describe all output sharing as impossible.

nodes.title: Requirements
nodes.purpose: Define what correct behavior and a safe change mean before choosing a service.
nodes.owns: Latency, allowed downtime/capacity loss, permissions, data lifetime and acceptable recovery.
nodes.handoff: Acceptance criteria become code/tests, release gates and production health checks.
nodes.boundary: Developer Associate focuses on implementing, testing and debugging applications; this map is a learning model, not a requirement to design an entire platform.
nodes.situation: Eight instances must keep serving during a batched rollout. “Some availability” is weaker than “full baseline capacity”.
nodes.evidence: Write the baseline, temporary-capacity budget and health/rollback criteria before picking a deployment policy.

nodes.title: Source / revision
nodes.purpose: Create an identifiable revision of the application, dependencies and infrastructure definition.
nodes.owns: Source revision and the trigger that starts an existing delivery workflow.
nodes.handoff: CodePipeline coordinates actions; a build action receives source and emits artifacts.
nodes.boundary: The pipeline is the coordinator. It does not itself replace the build environment or runtime application.
nodes.situation: A source commit exists, but there is no release execution. Inspect the source connection/trigger and execution revision.
nodes.evidence: Compare commit ID, source action result, trigger filters and pipeline execution history.

nodes.title: Build / test
nodes.purpose: Turn a revision into a tested artifact that the chosen runtime can execute.
nodes.owns: Buildspec commands, dependency packaging, unit/integration tests and immutable artifact identity.
nodes.handoff: A versioned ZIP/image/template goes to deployment. The runtime later executes that artifact; CodeBuild is not the production server.
nodes.boundary: Generated code/tests need review. Passing a build does not prove deployed IAM, integration behavior or production routing.
nodes.situation: The handler imports locally but fails after deployment. Check packaged files, runtime/architecture and dependency layout.
nodes.evidence: Build/test reports, artifact contents/digest and runtime import errors should refer to the same revision.

nodes.title: Provision / configure
nodes.purpose: Create or update the resources and configuration that a running application depends on.
nodes.owns: Declared resources, permissions, environment-specific values and resource lifecycle. Dynamic configuration has its own rollout.
nodes.handoff: The runtime receives resources/roles/settings; release promotion selects the application revision and traffic route.
nodes.boundary: CloudFormation can deploy application resources/code too. CodeDeploy adds specialized rollout behavior; they are complementary, not an absolute infrastructure/code split.
nodes.situation: The code is correct but a stack update changed the table/role configuration. Inspect stack events and resolved values.
nodes.evidence: Change set, stack events/outputs, runtime configuration and deployment-role permissions locate a provisioning failure.

nodes.title: Release / promote
nodes.purpose: Make an approved revision receive traffic using a controlled deployment strategy.
nodes.owns: Candidate version, deployment target, routing percentage, validation hooks and compatible rollback target.
nodes.handoff: A Lambda alias, API stage or fleet route makes a particular artifact serve user requests.
nodes.boundary: A published version is not automatically serving production. A canary routes a percentage; a parallel environment/fleet is a different isolation decision.
nodes.situation: The new package built successfully but users still see old behavior. Inspect the active alias/stage/fleet target.
nodes.evidence: Compare artifact/version with the actual endpoint route, deployment record and request-correlated version logs.

nodes.title: Verify / recover
nodes.purpose: Confirm that the deployed release works in its real environment, then recover or promote using evidence.
nodes.owns: Post-deploy business/health checks, alarms, release validation and rollback execution.
nodes.handoff: Production telemetry informs a rollback or the next code/configuration revision; it closes the application lifecycle loop.
nodes.boundary: A successful deployment job is not evidence of business correctness. Check compatibility of database/configuration changes during rollback.
nodes.situation: The canary passes a basic health URL but order creation fails. Validate the real integration before expanding traffic.
nodes.evidence: Deployment logs, critical-path tests, alarms, target health and the revision actually handling requests.

nodes.title: Client / caller
nodes.purpose: Make a request using the credential contract expected by the target.
nodes.owns: Request payload, client-visible timeout, correlation/request ID and user/machine identity.
nodes.handoff: The front door validates the caller; the backend later uses its own role to call AWS services.
nodes.boundary: A Cognito JWT is for a supported token-verifying target. Direct AWS SDK access generally needs temporary AWS credentials and a signed request.
nodes.situation: A mobile user signs in but a direct S3 call fails. Decide whether the client needs identity-pool credentials or should call the application API.
nodes.evidence: Inspect the actual target, token/credential type and issuer/audience/scope binding without logging secret values.

nodes.title: Trusted entry
nodes.purpose: Accept the request through a configured route and enforce the relevant entry controls.
nodes.owns: API stage/integration, request transformation, token validation or IAM authorization and traffic controls.
nodes.handoff: An authorized API invocation reaches the backend. Application code still checks business/record entitlement.
nodes.boundary: REST and HTTP API features differ. An API key for a usage plan is not user authentication; an ALB route is not an IAM grant.
nodes.situation: A request never reaches the Lambda handler. Check authorizer/access logs, stage deployment and integration permissions.
nodes.evidence: Distinguish entry 401/403, integration errors and backend errors before changing compute capacity.

nodes.title: Application code
nodes.purpose: Execute business logic against authorized data and downstream services.
nodes.owns: Input/business validation, tenant entitlement, AWS SDK calls, error handling and request-scoped context.
nodes.handoff: Read/write authoritative state, optionally publish background work, then construct the correct immediate response.
nodes.boundary: The caller and execution role are different principals. A runtime role can access a table while the app user is still forbidden from a particular record.
nodes.situation: The API authenticates correctly but the backend receives AccessDenied from DynamoDB. Inspect the backend role and target policies.
nodes.evidence: Correlate handler logs, role session, AWS action/resource and applicable policy denies; do not replace the caller token blindly.

nodes.title: State / cache
nodes.purpose: Persist authoritative data or reuse an appropriate cached copy.
nodes.owns: Access keys/indexes or SQL endpoints, consistency, projection, cache scope and lifetime.
nodes.handoff: Return data to the request path; background workers can update the same permitted state.
nodes.boundary: A replica/index/cache has a distinct consistency contract. TTL cleanup is asynchronous; a cache key must separate users/tenants where required.
nodes.situation: A user sees stale or another tenant’s cached result. Check authoritative state, cache key and invalidation before adding capacity.
nodes.evidence: Query/index or replica endpoint, projected fields, timestamps, cache hit/miss and tenant-scoped keys.

nodes.title: Response / outcome
nodes.purpose: Report what actually happened at the boundary the client is waiting for.
nodes.owns: Response schema/status, truthful operation state and a way to correlate or poll asynchronous work.
nodes.handoff: The caller receives success/failure or an accepted job ID. Telemetry records the request outcome.
nodes.boundary: A 202/accepted response or successfully published event does not prove the background business operation committed.
nodes.situation: The API accepts an order, but fulfillment runs later. Return a job/order identifier and expose actual status separately.
nodes.evidence: Match response semantics to the authoritative result record and trace/request ID.

nodes.title: Route / fan out
nodes.purpose: Deliver a publication to matching or subscribed consumers when routing/fanout is needed.
nodes.owns: Event schema, target selection, subscription/rule filters and publication/delivery errors.
nodes.handoff: Targets can be queues, functions or workflows. An application can also send directly to SQS/Kinesis without this routing stage.
nodes.boundary: Routing does not retain business-step progress. EventBridge bus types differ; select the exact feature contract rather than assuming identical guarantees.
nodes.situation: One publication must reach fulfillment and analytics independently. Fan out to separately authorized targets/queues.
nodes.evidence: Inspect publish results, rule/filter matches, target permissions and delivery/DLQ evidence.

nodes.title: Buffer / retain
nodes.purpose: Decouple producer and consumer capacity with a queue, or retain stream records for consumption/replay.
nodes.owns: Queue backlog/visibility/retention or stream partitioning/capacity and per-record ingestion outcomes.
nodes.handoff: A worker receives a job or stream record; successful receipt is not completed processing.
nodes.boundary: SQS and Kinesis are alternatives for different access/delivery needs. Inspect partial batch results and expect retries/duplicate side effects.
nodes.situation: PutRecords returns HTTP 200 with a failed entry. Retry that entry with backoff and investigate hot partition keys/capacity.
nodes.evidence: FailedRecordCount and result positions for Kinesis; queue age/backlog, visibility and DLQ for SQS.

nodes.title: Worker / workflow
nodes.purpose: Perform background work, using a state machine only when multi-step coordination is required.
nodes.owns: Task execution, workflow progress when used, bounded retries/catches and downstream failure handling.
nodes.handoff: Persist a recoverable business result before acknowledging the source; carry the request/event ID through every step.
nodes.boundary: A queue owns pending delivery; Step Functions owns workflow progress; Lambda/ECS executes code. CodePipeline belongs to software delivery.
nodes.situation: A payment call times out. Check the authoritative outcome before retrying, then recover using an idempotency key/result ledger.
nodes.evidence: Worker logs, workflow execution history, receive count and downstream request/operation identifiers.

nodes.title: Commit / acknowledge
nodes.purpose: Keep duplicate delivery from turning into duplicate business effects and report completion accurately.
nodes.owns: Atomic request claim, recorded result/status, recovery for abandoned work and acknowledgement ordering.
nodes.handoff: Committed state becomes visible to permitted readers; only then acknowledge according to the source/integration contract.
nodes.boundary: A conditional claim alone does not make an external payment exactly once. SQS deletion is not a database commit; Lambda event-source acknowledgements have their own contract.
nodes.situation: Two workers receive the same order. Use a conditional claim and persisted outcome; avoid a racing read-before-write check.
nodes.evidence: Request ledger, condition failure, business result and acknowledgement timing show whether work is duplicated or lost.

nodes.title: Identity / authorization
nodes.purpose: Apply separate identity and access decisions to delivery, users and machine workloads.
nodes.owns: Developer/deployment roles, API token trust, backend/worker roles and application-level entitlements.
nodes.handoff: Each trust boundary validates the correct principal/credential and permits only its intended action and data.
nodes.boundary: The deployment role does not become the end user. Boundaries/SCPs restrict applicable grants; a valid JWT is not automatically an AWS permission.
nodes.situation: The front door accepts a token but the app leaks another tenant’s record. Enforce record entitlement at the application/data access boundary.
nodes.evidence: Token claims, route scopes, execution-role action/resource and tenant-filter decisions are distinct evidence.

nodes.title: Secrets / protection
nodes.purpose: Protect configuration, credentials and data without confusing protection with permission.
nodes.owns: Secret rotation/retrieval, encryption keys, TLS/private paths and sensitive-data handling.
nodes.handoff: Delivery configures references and policies; authorized runtime code retrieves values and uses protected resources.
nodes.boundary: Encrypted data is not automatically authorized data. A security group permits a network path, not an IAM action or a business operation.
nodes.situation: The application keeps using a rotated password. Check runtime secret retrieval/cache behavior and the database integration.
nodes.evidence: Secret version/rotation status, retrieval errors, KMS access and connection evidence; sanitize diagnostic logs.

nodes.title: Resilience / performance
nodes.purpose: Keep failures bounded and match capacity to the measured bottleneck.
nodes.owns: Timeout budgets, backoff/jitter, idempotency, concurrency, worker scaling and safe caching.
nodes.handoff: Pressure/failure signals guide application/configuration changes and subsequent release validation.
nodes.boundary: More capacity does not repair a policy deny or invalid request. Retries increase pressure unless paired with limits and idempotency.
nodes.situation: Queue depth grows while workers are busy. Compare backlog per worker and processing time; investigate downstream throttling before scaling blindly.
nodes.evidence: Queue age, backlog per worker, duration/concurrency/throttles and downstream capacity reveal the limiting stage.

nodes.title: Observability / feedback
nodes.purpose: Gather enough evidence to locate the first failed boundary and validate a change.
nodes.owns: Structured logs, correlated requests/versions, metrics/alarms, traces and AWS API-change evidence.
nodes.handoff: Production outcomes feed Verify/recover and the next code/configuration change; this closes the lifecycle loop.
nodes.boundary: Metrics show trends, access logs show requests, traces locate stages and CloudTrail shows covered AWS API activity. Configure the evidence before an incident.
nodes.situation: Latency rises after release. Compare versions and a correlated trace before changing memory, replicas or queue capacity.
nodes.evidence: Use the symptom’s metric to find the window, then request logs/spans, then relevant deployment/configuration events.

edges.label: Publish job / event · Optional async path

scenarios.title: Build passed; production still runs old code
scenarios.prompt: The build produced revision B, but production requests still log revision A.
scenarios.evidence: Compare the build artifact/digest with the alias, API deployment/stage or fleet route used by a correlated production request.
scenarios.decision: Fix the release target or route. Rebuilding the same artifact does not promote it to production.
scenarios.change: If the live route already uses B, inspect the request path/cache and actual packaged content instead.

scenarios.title: Canary breaks the order path
scenarios.prompt: A new version passes the basic health URL, but the order operation starts failing during a canary.
scenarios.evidence: Check critical-path results, deployment hooks/alarms, downstream errors and the candidate version handling each request.
scenarios.decision: Stop expansion and use the configured recovery/rollback path; then fix the first failing integration or configuration boundary.
scenarios.change: If both versions fail identically and no release-specific change is implicated, investigate shared dependencies before blaming the candidate.

scenarios.title: Sign-in works; backend AWS call is denied
scenarios.prompt: The API accepts the user token, but the Lambda function receives AccessDenied when writing an order.
scenarios.evidence: Identify the execution-role session, action/resource, resource/key policy and applicable explicit denies. Separate this from user token validation.
scenarios.decision: Grant only the required backend operation through the correct policies and guardrails. Keep application entitlement checks in place.
scenarios.change: A rejected/expired API token fails at Trusted entry instead; the handler may never run.

scenarios.title: API accepts work; the business result is missing
scenarios.prompt: The API returns an accepted job ID, but a worker removes the queue message before persisting a recoverable result and then crashes.
scenarios.evidence: Correlate event/request ID, queue receipt/acknowledgement, worker error and authoritative result record.
scenarios.decision: Make result/acknowledgement ordering recoverable and idempotent. An accepted response is not a completed outcome.
scenarios.change: If the event never reached the intended queue, inspect publish results, routing/filter matches and delivery permissions earlier in the path.

scenarios.title: HTTP 200; one stream record failed
scenarios.prompt: The producer receives HTTP 200 from PutRecords with FailedRecordCount = 1.
scenarios.evidence: Match each result to the corresponding input entry; inspect the error, partition keys and stream capacity.
scenarios.decision: Retry failed entries with exponential backoff and jitter; correct hot-key/capacity pressure rather than resending successes immediately.
scenarios.change: A consumer-side failure after successful ingestion needs consumer checkpoint/retry handling, not a producer ingestion fix.

scenarios.title: The same order is processed twice
scenarios.prompt: Duplicate delivery or a timeout causes two workers to attempt the same business operation.
scenarios.evidence: Check the request ID, atomic claim/result ledger and the authoritative downstream outcome before retrying.
scenarios.decision: Use conditional idempotency control plus persisted status/results and recovery. A read-before-write check can race.
scenarios.change: If duplicate execution has no side effect and is acceptable, the operation may not need the same coordination overhead.

scenarios.title: A request becomes slow after release
scenarios.prompt: End-to-end latency increases, but the bottleneck has not been identified.
scenarios.evidence: Use metrics to find the window and version, then correlated spans/logs to separate entry, compute, data and downstream wait.
scenarios.decision: Tune the measured boundary: memory/CPU, concurrency, key/query access, cache, replica routing or worker capacity as appropriate.
scenarios.change: If the request is rejected by authentication or health configuration, performance tuning is not the first repair.

scenarios.title: Valid token; wrong tenant’s record
scenarios.prompt: A legitimate user can request another tenant’s record through an authenticated API.
scenarios.evidence: Inspect record entitlement, tenant filter/key, cache scope and the authorization decision at the data-access boundary.
scenarios.decision: Enforce application-level tenant/record authorization. Token validity and a broad backend role do not establish that entitlement.
scenarios.change: If the backend IAM action itself is denied, inspect service permissions separately; that is a different boundary.
